text:
Five habits that stop most scams

1. Pause. Scammers want you to act fast.
2. Verify through a second channel, such as calling a number you already trust.
3. Never share passwords, PINs or one-time codes.
4. Keep your phone updated; install updates only from the official store.
5. Talk to someone. Fraud depends on secrecy, so describe the message to a friend or relative before you act. If you think you have been scammed, tell your bank at once; speed matters.

Take the full training at https://learn.example.org/awareness.

Victim story: 'I nearly lost my savings'

Grace from Takoradi received a call from a man who claimed to be from the telecom company. He said her SIM would be blocked unless she confirmed a code that arrives by SMS. She felt panic, but remembered the awareness poster at her workplace. She hung up, called the official customer-care line and learned there was no such problem. 'The code was for my mobile money wallet,' she says. 'If I had read it aloud, everything would have gone.' She now tells everyone she knows.

text: Romance scams explained. The fraudster builds a relationship online, often over weeks, using stolen photos. Eventually there is a problem: a hospital bill, a customs fee, a ticket to visit. They ask you to send money, usually by gift card or transfer. Warning signs include refusing video calls, moving the chat to a private app quickly and asking for secrecy. If someone you have never met asks for money, stop contact, keep the messages as evidence and report the profile to the platform. It is not your fault; these criminals are professionals. How scammers trick you: the urgency trap

Fraudsters rely on pressure. They send a message saying your account will be closed in 24 hours unless you verify your details through a link. Real banks do not work this way. Lakeview Bank will never ask for your PIN, password or one-time code, and will never ask you to install a remote-access app. If you receive such a message, do not tap the link, do not reply, and call the number on the back of your card. Report it and then delete it. Share this post with a relative who is not comfortable with technology. Remember: no genuine organisation will pressure you to act immediately.

Participants who were busy or worried were twice as likely to follow a fake instruction to verify an account. Five habits that stop most scams

1. Pause. Scammers want you to act fast.
2. Verify through a second channel, such as calling a number you already trust.
3. Never share passwords, PINs or one-time codes.
4. Keep your phone updated; install updates only from the official store.
5. Talk to someone. Fraud depends on secrecy, so describe the message to a friend or relative before you act. If you think you have been scammed, tell your bank at once; speed matters. Share this with friends and family.

How scammers trick you: the urgency trap

Fraudsters rely on pressure. They send a message saying your account will be closed in 24 hours unless you verify your details through a link. Real banks do not work this way. Lakeview Bank will never ask for your PIN, password or one-time code, and will never ask you to install a remote-access app. If you receive such a message, do not tap the link, do not reply, and call the number on the back of your card. Report it and then delete it. Share this post with a relative who is not comfortable with technology. Take the full training at https://learn.example.org/awareness.

Romance scams explained. The fraudster builds a relationship online, often over weeks, using stolen photos. Eventually there is a problem: a hospital bill, a customs fee, a ticket to visit. They ask you to send money, usually by gift card or transfer. Warning signs include refusing video calls, moving the chat to a private app quickly and asking for secrecy. If someone you have never met asks for money, stop contact, keep the messages as evidence and report the profile to the platform. It is not your fault; these criminals are professionals.

Awareness is the best protection against fraud.
